props.title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom

sections.content: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom stands as Pier Paolo Pasolini's final and most controversial film, using Marquis de Sade's philosophy to create a brutal critique of fascism. Pasolini transposes de Sade's 18th-century story to the Italian Social Republic of 1944-1945, where four powerful men subject 16 young people to escalating torture. The film is notoriously difficult to watch, but its artistic merit lies in exposing how power structures enable dehumanization. Pasolini, who was murdered shortly before the film's release, crafted each frame with painterly precision, drawing from Renaissance art and Dante's Inferno.

sections.content: The film's influence reverberates through controversial cinema that examines power and corruption. Caligula (1979) attempted similar themes but descended into exploitation. Michael Haneke's Funny Games (1997) and its 2007 remake challenged audience complicity in on-screen violence, while The Act of Killing (2012) documented real perpetrators of political violence recreating their crimes. SUBHEAD: Artistic Legacy and Critical Theory

Contemporary filmmakers continue grappling with Salò's themes of institutional power and moral corruption. The White Ribbon (2009) examines the roots of fascism through a similar lens of controlled violence. Antichrist (2009) and The House That Jack Built (2018) by Lars von Trier push boundaries of depicting evil while maintaining artistic purpose. These films demonstrate how Pasolini's work opened discussions about representing political violence in cinema.
